overview: Foley Wines is a New Zealand-listed, vertically integrated premium wine producer operating six wineries and a distillery across Marlborough (Grove Mill, Vavasour), Martinborough (Martinborough Vineyard, Te Kairanga, Lighthouse Gin) and Central Otago (Mt Difficulty), supplemented by cellar-door/hospitality venues including The Runholder. It sells bottled wine domestically and to export markets (USA, UK/Europe, Australia, Asia/Pacific) under a 'premiumisation' strategy that avoids the commodity bulk-wine market. The company is majority controlled (52.80%) by Foley Holdings New Zealand Limited, itself 80.47%-owned by FFW Opco, LLC (a US entity associated with businessman William P Foley II, founder of Fidelity National Financial/Cannae), making it a controlled micro-cap with limited free float and heavy related-party dealing.

business_model.summary: Revenue comes from bottled wine sales through wholesale/distributor channels in export markets and direct/retail channels domestically, plus a smaller hospitality/cellar-door and bulk-wine/spirits/merchandise revenue line. The company owns vineyards and wineries (capital intensive, long inventory-ageing cycles) rather than solely contract-sourcing grapes, giving it control over quality but exposing it to biological-asset fair-value swings, vineyard revaluations and harvest variability. FY2026 (year to 30 June 2026) total revenue was NZ$67.868m (down 4% from NZ$70.582m FY2025), with bottled wine sales NZ$62.800m (down 5.4%) on lower case sales of 552,000 9L cases (down 9.5% from FY2025's record 610,000), while average net revenue per case improved 4.7% reflecting a richer premium mix; management describes FY2026 as a deliberate trade-off of volume for margin and inventory clearance after the industry-wide 2025 oversupply. Management treats 'operating earnings' (profit before interest, impairment and IAS 41 revaluation gains/losses) as the key internal metric because IAS 41 fair-value movements on harvested grapes are non-cash and simply reverse between the harvest year and the sale year.

revenue_streams.name: Bottled wine sales (branded, premium)
revenue_streams.trend: case volumes declining as strategy shifts to price/mix over volume; net revenue per case +4.7% FY2026

business_model.customer_type: B2B distributor/wholesale for export markets plus B2C retail, cellar-door and hospitality domestically; not a bulk/commodity supplier by strategy
business_model.geographic_mix: FY2026 bottled case sales: New Zealand 164,000 cases (30%, -4%), UK/Europe 147,000 (27%, +2%, outpacing the market), USA 103,000 (19%, -10%, tariff-affected), Australia 76,000 (14%, -26%, consumers swinging to locally produced product), Asia/Pacific 58,000 (10%, -21% but China delivered growth within the region), Rest of World 4,000 (1%, -20%); total 552,000 cases, down 9.5% on FY2025's record 610,000. H1 FY2026 (Jul-Dec 2025) showed export sales +1% and domestic -10%, with case volumes recovering somewhat through H2 as the 2026 vintage began shipping.

main_competitors: Numerous independent Marlborough/Central Otago producers amid a fragmented, oversupplied industry
competitive_position.market_position: Small-cap, multi-region premium portfolio player (~NZ$68m revenue) versus much larger scaled competitors (Delegat, Constellation, Pernod Ricard, Indevin) with far greater balance sheet strength and bulk/contract flexibility; FWL's stated edge is a multi-region 'one-stop' brand portfolio (Marlborough, Martinborough, Central Otago) that lets distributors source varied varietals and price points from one supplier, and management explicitly cites production across three regions as a competitive advantage from both a weather-risk and consumer-portfolio perspective.

moat_factors.description: Six recognised regional brands spanning three acclaimed wine regions gives distribution partners a broader assortment than single-region rivals; FY2026 wine-show results included Champion Sauvignon Blanc trophies for Te Kairanga and Vavasour, plus 17 wines scoring 90+ points from James Suckling and a hatted restaurant award for The Runholder.

Vertical integration (vineyards + wineries + cellar doors) gives quality control and asset backing (NTA/share NZ$1.65 vs NZ$0.56 share price) but ties up capital and cannot flex down quickly when demand falls.

Management cites 'strong distribution partnerships' in UK and Asia (China delivered growth again in FY2026) and cross-supply/promotional support with related party Foley Family Wines USA as a source of resilience against a difficult US tariff environment.

Refusing to dump into the bulk-wine glut protects brand value but means FWL absorbs inventory carrying costs and higher promotional spend (selling/marketing/promotion expense rose to NZ$9.571m in FY2026 from NZ$9.254m) rather than clearing stock quickly, and it still cannot avoid industry-wide price competition on branded product.

weaknesses: Sub-scale relative to major NZ wine groups (Delegat, Indevin, Constellation) with less bargaining power on grape sourcing, freight and retailer listing fees

Illiquid NZX micro-cap (~NZ$37m market cap at NZ$0.56/share) with a controlling shareholder holding 52.80% (indirectly ~42.5% via FFW Opco), leaving a thin free float and wide bid/ask spreads on light trading volumes
High fixed-cost, capital-intensive vineyard/winery asset base that cannot be quickly resized when the industry cycle turns down

Earnings quality distorted year to year by non-cash IAS 41 biological-asset revaluations (FY2026 unrealised loss on harvested grapes of NZ$3,187,000, worse than FY2025's NZ$1,317,000) and periodic property revaluation write-downs

Case volumes are now falling for a second consecutive reporting period (down 9.5% FY2026 after a record FY2025) even as the company recovers margin, indicating real demand/competitive pressure in the US, Australia and Asia/Pacific markets, not just a self-directed pivot

growth_drivers: Margin-over-volume repositioning bearing fruit: average net revenue per case up 4.7% in FY2026 and operating earnings up 323.5% to NZ$5.878m, evidence that premiumisation and promotional discipline are rebuilding profitability even with lower case sales
UK/Europe momentum continuing to outpace the broader market (+2% FY2026 cases on top of +8% FY2025) via strong distribution partnerships

China/Asia-Pacific remains a stated 'major focus' with continued growth in China specifically, even though the broader Asia/Pacific region case count fell FY2026 off a very strong FY2025 comparative (+115%)

Hospitality/brand-home expansion (The Runholder in Martinborough — awarded a Cuisine Good Food Awards 'Hat' in FY2026 — and Mt Difficulty Cellar Door and Restaurant) building direct-to-consumer margin, event/wedding revenue and brand equity; the reimagined single-venue Toast Martinborough festival (headlined by Sir Dave Dobbyn) sold out in two weeks and will be an annual fixture at The Runholder

Vineyard replanting programme improving varietal mix continues, alongside a completed Vavasour winery wastewater treatment upgrade (the major FY2026 capex item) and ongoing Central Otago frost-protection investment

Signs the industry oversupply cycle may be beginning to turn: FY2026 New Zealand-wide harvest was reported down materially on 2025 (FWL's own harvest -7% to 8,012 tonnes), described by some industry voices as a 'welcome correction'; a rebalancing of grape/bulk pricing and reduced discounting would flow through with significant operating leverage given FWL's largely fixed cost base

Continued deleveraging (net loans and borrowings down from NZ$52.5m FY2024 to NZ$40.6m FY2025 to ~NZ$35.5m FY2026) freeing future cash flow from interest costs; net finance costs fell from NZ$3.599m FY2025 to NZ$2.436m FY2026
Management guiding to a 'normal vintage' in 2027 and 'cautiously optimistic' commentary for improved market conditions ahead

business.risk: Structural NZ/global wine oversupply and price competition, now compounded by weather-driven cost pressure
business.description: The 2026 unrealised loss on harvested grapes (NZ$3,187,000, up from NZ$1,317,000 FY2025) reflected both a lower Marlborough/Martinborough market grape price (continued fallout of the very large 2022/2023/2025 harvests) AND adverse growing-season weather that raised the cost per tonne to produce FWL's own grapes — a double squeeze on margin from the biological-asset revaluation. Deep discounting across the industry drove higher promotional spend to keep FWL's own case volumes moving.

business.risk: Case volume decline across most export markets
business.description: FY2026 bottled case sales fell 9.5% to 552,000, with USA -10%, Australia -26% (consumers swinging to local product) and Asia/Pacific -21% (against a very strong FY2025 comparative); only UK/Europe (+2%) grew. Management frames this as a deliberate quality-over-volume trade-off, but sustained volume erosion in three of five regions is also consistent with genuine competitive/demand pressure.

Adverse weather in Marlborough and Martinborough during the FY2026 growing season and harvest reduced yields and raised cost per tonne; the FY2026 total harvest fell 7% to 8,012 tonnes from 8,638 tonnes in FY2025 (which itself followed a 21% harvest decline in FY2024 to 6,404 tonnes).

Extensive related-party dealings with Foley Family Wines USA (the US distributor and part-owner of FWL's controlling shareholder chain), Wharekauhau Country Estate, Foley Hospitality Ltd and Lighthouse Distillery Ltd create potential conflicts of interest, though all are disclosed; H1 FY2026 accounts recorded NZ$204,000 of related-party tariff-related discounts.

financial.risk: Leverage against a still-modest earnings base
financial.description: Total loans and borrowings were NZ$35.492m (NZ$4.992m current + NZ$30.500m non-current) at 30 June 2026 against operating EBITDA that recovered to NZ$15.502m (up 22.8% from NZ$12.628m FY2025); leverage is now more comfortably covered than at the FY2025 trough, and interest expense fell to NZ$2.483m (from NZ$3.642m FY2025) on lower rates and lower balances.

financial.risk: Convertible note and bank facility renewal
financial.description: A NZ$10.9m related-party convertible note (held by Foley Holdings New Zealand Limited) remains in current liabilities at 30 June 2026 unchanged from FY2025; the BNZ banking facility renewed in August 2023 for a 3-year term falls due for renewal around August 2026 — a refinancing event that should now be assessed against a materially improved FY2026 earnings and cash-flow picture than a year ago.

No property revaluation decrement was recorded in FY2026 (versus a NZ$4.607m decrement in FY2025), but IAS 41 biological-asset fair-value swings remain a material and growing source of non-cash volatility (unrealised loss of NZ$3,187,000 in FY2026 vs NZ$1,317,000 in FY2025) that can mislead investors reading only headline NPAT.

A 2.0 cents per share fully imputed final dividend was again declared for FY2026 (matching FY2025's resumed payment after a nil FY2024 final), but the Board continues to explicitly prioritise debt reduction over larger distributions 'over the next 12 months', with no explicit numeric forward dividend target.

regulatory.description: The US is NZ wine's largest export market (~NZ$762m of exports in the year to June 2025, over one-third of total NZ wine export earnings, though value to the US has since fallen ~5% to ~NZ$720.6m). A 10% reciprocal tariff took effect 5 April 2025, and from 24 July 2026 a Section 122 adjustment set the rate at 12.5% for New Zealand (among 41 economies deemed not to sufficiently prohibit forced-labour imports, versus 10% for the UK/Canada/Mexico), bringing the total effective US duty on NZ wine to roughly 17% including the pre-existing ~4.5% MFN rate. Wine was not among the NZ products (e.g., beef, kiwifruit) granted exemptions. FWL's USA case sales fell 10% in FY2026 and management explicitly cites ongoing tariff-driven challenges, while noting a plan with Foley Family Wines USA to return to growth.

Excise duty and Health Promotion Agency levy costs are a direct, non-negotiable cost line embedded in cost of sales; further increases in NZ or export-market alcohol excise/duty would compress margins.

macro.risk: Consumer downtrading and declining alcohol consumption
macro.description: Global and NZ per-capita wine consumption has been declining, particularly among younger demographics, compounding the industry oversupply; weak NZ discretionary retail spending was again cited as a factor in FY2026 domestic sales softness (-4% cases).

Revenue is earned in USD, GBP, EUR and AUD against an NZD cost base (vineyards, wineries, NZ payroll); FX movements directly affect reported NZD revenue and margin, and the Group's unrealised fair-value loss on financial assets/liabilities (largely FX derivatives) was NZ$885,000 in FY2026.

As a leveraged capital-intensive producer, FWL has benefited directly from NZ interest rate declines and reduced borrowings (net finance costs down from NZ$3.599m FY2025 to NZ$2.436m FY2026) but remains exposed if rates were to rise again.

Glass, packaging and insurance costs have been rising, partially offset by the transition to 'super lightweight' bottles (now covering nearly three-quarters of finished packaged wine) and continued solar-generation investment (Meridian CER partnership) reducing energy costs.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The NZ wine industry, and Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc in particular, has been working through a structural oversupply built up over the large 2022, 2023 and 2025 harvests, compounded by softening global demand since COVID. The FY2026 (2026 vintage) national and FWL-specific harvests came in materially smaller than 2025 (FWL down 7% to 8,012 tonnes), which some industry commentary describes as a 'welcome correction'; there is emerging debate in trade press (September 2026) over whether the situation is better characterised as a US demand/allocation problem than a pure oversupply problem, alongside continued diversification into higher-value varieties like Pinot Noir. A full rebalancing is still expected to take years at only 1-2% annual demand growth rather than a quick snapback, but FY2026 results (operating earnings +323.5%, operating EBITDA +22.8%) suggest the worst of the margin compression for FWL specifically may be past.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — agricultural production cycle (weather-dependent annual harvest) layered on top of a multi-year industry destocking cycle and consumer-discretionary demand sensitivity
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate given leverage (~NZ$35.5m bank debt plus NZ$10.9m convertible note plus ~NZ$10.8m lease liabilities against NZ$143.6m equity at 30 June 2026), though declining rates and reduced balances have been a net tailwind through FY2026

recent_developments.event: FY2026 annual report published (year ended 30 June 2026): total revenue NZ$67.868m (down 4%), bottled sales revenue NZ$62.800m (down 5.4%) on case sales of 552,000 (down 9.5% from FY2025's record 610,000), average net revenue per case up 4.7%; operating earnings surged 323.5% to NZ$5.878m, operating EBITDA up 22.8% to NZ$15.502m, and profit after tax up 258.2% to NZ$2.937m (vs a NZ$1.857m loss in FY2025); no property revaluation decrement recorded (vs NZ$4.607m in FY2025); a 2.0 cps fully imputed final dividend was declared, matching FY2025; termination benefits for the former CEO were paid during the year.

Board announced Tony Anselmi, an independent director since September 2012 (14 years' tenure), will retire at the conclusion of the November 2026 AGM and will not seek re-election — following the NZ Shareholders' Association's prior recommendation against his re-election on board-renewal grounds.

2026 harvest result announcement: total harvest of 8,012 tonnes, down 7% on FY2025's 8,638 tonnes; preliminary indications were for the 2026 Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc grape price to be materially below the FY2025 average of NZ$1,812/tonne, and the stock fell sharply on the news at the time.

H1 FY2026 (six months to 31 Dec 2025) result released: revenue NZ$34.916m, operating earnings NZ$2.649m (+30.2%), reported NPAT NZ$2.300m (+112%), operating EBITDA NZ$7.607m (down 3.8%), operating cash flow NZ$6.709m (down 39% YoY on receivables timing and higher promotional spend); export sales +1%, domestic sales -10%.

Annual Shareholders Meeting held at The Runholder, Martinborough; William P Foley II was re-elected as a Non-Independent Director with only ~90.96% support (~8.6% against/withheld), a notable minority protest vote for a controlling shareholder's board seat.

US Section 122 tariff adjustment set New Zealand's rate at 12.5% (New Zealand was among 41 economies assessed as not sufficiently prohibiting forced-labour imports, versus 10% for the UK/Canada/Mexico), taking the total effective US duty on NZ wine to roughly 17% including the pre-existing ~4.5% MFN base rate; wine was not among the NZ products granted tariff exemptions.

Industry trade press debate emerging over whether the NZ Sauvignon Blanc 'oversupply' narrative is shifting to a US demand/allocation issue, alongside reports of a materially smaller 2026 national harvest being read as a positive correction for the multi-year destocking cycle.

items.target: Approximately NZ$3.7m for FY2027, in line with the average of the past two years and below depreciation expense
items.vs_prior: lowered slightly (from ~NZ$4.5m guided for FY2026, actual FY2026 capex was NZ$3.907m)
items.notes: Continued investment in Central Otago vineyard development/frost protection and replacement of aging viticulture equipment; the major one-off item (Vavasour wastewater treatment plant) is now complete

items.target: No explicit forward numeric dividend target; Board states it will evaluate present and projected cash flows, sustainable operating earnings and capital/acquisition requirements each period, with continued priority on reducing debt over the next 12 months
items.notes: FY2026 final dividend of 2.0 cps fully imputed matched FY2025's resumed payment

items.target: Management expresses hope for a 'normal vintage' in 2027 and describes itself as 'cautiously optimistic' about improved market conditions, without providing numeric yield or price guidance
items.vs_prior: no prior comparable numeric guidance; qualitative tone improved versus FY2026 commentary
items.notes: Company says it is 'well positioned to sell through the 2026 vintage in a timely manner' with inventory 'generally in balance'

items.target: No quantitative revenue/earnings guidance issued for FY2027; management cites continued economic uncertainty and weather risk but expresses confidence in the premiumisation strategy, cost discipline and distribution partnerships, and frames three-region production as a competitive advantage for both weather-risk diversification and portfolio breadth
items.vs_prior: improved tone versus FY2025/FY2026 commentary, though still no numeric targets
items.notes: H1 FY2027 result (six months to 31 Dec 2026) is the next scheduled disclosure event, expected around late February 2027

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Mike Higgins (FY2026 annual report): 'The year was very challenging off the back of a bumper 2025 harvest and a well-documented oversupply of New Zealand wine available, resulting in a very competitive marketplace and deep discounting... this investment [in promotional funding] was a major factor in the increase in selling, marketing and promotion expenses, however, this has meant the Company is already shipping the 2026 vintage to many markets and our inventory is generally in balance.' On outlook: 'The Company has significant confidence in its business model and the team it has built. The Company is in good shape and well positioned to sell through the 2026 vintage in a timely manner. With the hope of a normal vintage in 2027 and improved market conditions, we are cautiously optimistic for the future.'

bull_case: FY2026 delivered a sharp, broad-based earnings recovery (operating earnings +323.5% to NZ$5.878m, operating EBITDA +22.8% to NZ$15.502m, NPAT +258.2% to NZ$2.937m) even while case volumes fell, evidencing genuine margin repair via premiumisation, cost discipline and reduced discounting rather than a one-off

Balance sheet materially strengthened: net loans and borrowings down from ~NZ$52.5m (FY2024) to ~NZ$40.6m (FY2025) to ~NZ$35.5m (FY2026), net finance costs down from NZ$3.599m to NZ$2.436m, and no property revaluation decrement in FY2026, reducing financial risk into any further industry recovery

Asset-backed valuation support persists: net tangible assets of ~NZ$1.65/share versus a ~NZ$0.56 share price still implies a large discount to book, with owned vineyards, wineries and hospitality venues (The Runholder, Mt Difficulty Cellar Door) providing tangible collateral; the stock has already re-rated from a 2026 low near NZ$0.43 to ~NZ$0.56-0.60

Early, if tentative, signs the multi-year NZ wine oversupply cycle is turning: the FY2026 national and FWL harvests came in well below 2025 levels, described by some industry voices as a 'welcome correction', with management's own commentary shifting to 'cautiously optimistic' for a 'normal' 2027 vintage
UK/Europe and China continue to outperform, and a resumed/maintained 2.0 cps fully imputed dividend (yielding ~5% at current price) rewards holders while debt reduction remains the stated priority
bear_case: Case volumes fell for a second straight year (-9.5% in FY2026 to 552,000, following a record FY2025), with declines in three of five markets (USA -10%, Australia -26%, Asia/Pacific -21%) — the margin recovery has so far come from price/mix and cost control, not demand growth, and a further leg of the 'oversupply is turning' thesis is still unconfirmed

US tariffs, now effectively ~17% including MFN duty following the July 2026 Section 122 adjustment, directly hit FWL's largest single export market and show no sign of near-term relief; wine remains excluded from the categories (beef, kiwifruit) that secured exemptions

Governance and liquidity structure remains a persistent overhang: Foley Holdings New Zealand Limited controls 52.80% of the register (itself 80.47%-owned by a US entity linked to William P Foley II), leaving a thin free float, an illiquid NZX micro-cap (~NZ$37m market cap), extensive related-party transactions, and a board that saw a controlling shareholder's own re-election draw a meaningful ~8.6% protest vote in November 2025

Earnings quality remains volatile and hard to read headline-to-headline: FY2026's unrealised loss on harvested grapes (NZ$3,187,000) was larger than FY2025's (NZ$1,317,000), reflecting both falling grape prices and weather-driven higher production costs, and the dividend was cut to zero as recently as FY2024 in this same downturn

The BNZ banking facility (renewed August 2023 for a 3-year term) falls due for renewal around August 2026, and a NZ$10.9m related-party convertible note remains classified as a current liability — refinancing risk persists even though FY2026's improved earnings and cash generation put the company in a stronger negotiating position than a year earlier
